overview:
Taiwan's AI Basic Act passed the Legislative Yuan in December 2025 and took effect on 14 January 2026, adopting an EU-AI-Act-aligned definition of AI and seven core principles: sustainable development and wellbeing, human autonomy, privacy, cybersecurity, transparency, fairness, and accountability. The Act also requires the Executive Yuan to form a national AI strategy committee to draft Taiwan's first AI development blueprint, though its current operational status (fully constituted versus still forming) is not yet clearly confirmed.

Compared with most peer economies profiled here, Taiwan's AI story is often framed around chips rather than models — TSMC's role in the global AI hardware supply chain appears to receive far more policy and media attention than any domestic frontier AI software lab, and Taiwan does not currently appear to have a lab operating at a scale comparable to Japan's Sakana AI or France's Mistral. As of mid-2026, Taiwan is reportedly considering export-control rules on AI chips to China that go beyond the existing US blacklist, with potential implications for TSMC and its supply chain if adopted.

debates.topic: AI chip export controls on China beyond the existing US blacklist
debates.summary: Taiwan is reportedly considering export restrictions on AI chips to China that go further than current US rules — a move that, if adopted, could have significant consequences for TSMC and its server-maker customers.
debates.expanded: Because TSMC manufactures a large share of the world's most advanced AI chips, any Taiwanese export-control decision could have outsized global impact compared with a similar decision by most other governments. Server makers like Foxconn could face supply-chain risk if restrictions tighten further, while some national-security-focused commentators argue Taiwan has an incentive to align closely with US controls given its own security relationship with Washington.

debates.topic: Building an AI ecosystem around chips rather than models
debates.summary: Taiwan's AI policy conversation appears to be shaped more by hardware and supply-chain questions than by model development or deployment risk, in contrast to many peer economies.
debates.expanded: Unlike most economies profiled here, Taiwan does not appear to have a domestic frontier AI software lab of comparable scale to build policy around — its AI Basic Act and the planned national AI strategy committee are intended to define what an AI development blueprint looks like for an economy whose comparative advantage lies in manufacturing chips that other countries' AI models run on, rather than in building the models themselves.
